outline.section: H2: What Actually Makes a Body Lotion Work?
outline.guidance: Explain the three functional components of any effective body lotion: humectants (draw moisture in), emollients (soften and smooth), and occlusives (seal moisture in). Use plain language. Give brief examples of each type of ingredient — e.g., glycerin and aloe as humectants; plant oils (coconut oil, jojoba) as emollients; shea butter or beeswax as occlusives. Explain why many budget lotion brands rely heavily on water and synthetic emollients like petrolatum derivatives, which can sit on top of skin without true nourishment. Cite a credible dermatological or academic source for the humectant/emollient/occlusive framework (e.g., American Academy of Dermatology or a peer-reviewed dermatology journal). This section establishes the evaluative criteria used throughout the rest of the post. Include 'body lotion for dry skin', 'moisturizing body lotion', and 'body butter' naturally.

outline.section: H2: The Ingredient Red Flags to Watch in Any Lotion Brand
outline.guidance: This is the 'What to Avoid' section — a unique content block not covered by any current top-10 competitor. Cover 4–5 specific ingredients or ingredient categories to avoid and briefly explain why each is problematic: (1) Synthetic fragrance — often a cocktail of undisclosed chemicals, a common skin irritant and allergen; cite EWG or a peer-reviewed allergy/dermatology source. (2) Parabens — preservatives with endocrine-disruption concerns; cite a credible source such as the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences or a published study. (3) Mineral oil and petrolatum derivatives — occlusive but derived from petroleum, may block pores; note that some dermatologists consider certain grades safe, so present this nuanced rather than as absolute. (4) Artificial colorants — no skin benefit, potential irritant. (5) High water content with low active ingredient concentration — a formulation red flag. Keep tone informative and empowering, not alarmist. Naturally incorporate 'body lotion without chemicals', 'fragrance free body lotion', 'clean ingredient body lotion', and 'all natural lotion'.

outline.section: H2: How to Choose the Right Lotion Brand for Your Skin Type
outline.guidance: Provide a concise decision framework — essentially a 'how to choose' guide within the listicle. Use a skin-type mapping approach: (1) Normal to slightly dry skin → lightweight natural lotion with glycerin and plant oils. (2) Very dry or cracked skin → body butter or rich cream with coconut oil or shea. (3) Sensitive or allergy-prone → fragrance-free, short ingredient list, patch-test first. (4) Oily or acne-prone body skin → lightweight, non-comedogenic formula; avoid heavy occlusive butters on acne-prone areas. (5) Aging or crepey skin → look for occlusives plus antioxidants (vitamin E, plant polyphenols). Keep this section practical and scannable — consider using a short bulleted list for each skin type. Link to the body lotion for dry skin collection and the organic hand lotion collection for hand-specific needs. Include 'best body lotion', 'hand lotion', 'moisturizing body lotion'.

outline.section: H2: Frequently Asked Questions About Lotion Brands
outline.guidance: Include 4 concise FAQ items targeting high-volume semantic queries and common decision-stage questions. Each answer should be 2–4 sentences. Suggested questions: (1) What lotion brand is best for extremely dry skin? — Answer should emphasize ingredient criteria (thick occlusives, plant oils, fragrance-free) and point to Real Skin Care's body lotion for dry skin collection. (2) Are natural lotion brands actually better for your skin? — Honest, evidence-referenced answer: ingredient quality matters more than the 'natural' label; look for certified organic, short ingredient lists, no synthetic fragrance. (3) What's the difference between body lotion and body butter? — Lotion is lighter (more water), body butter is denser (more oils/butters); body butter is better for very dry or crepey skin. (4) Is coconut oil a good moisturizer? — Yes, particularly for emollient benefits due to lauric acid content; formulated lotions that combine it with humectants provide more comprehensive hydration than coconut oil alone. citation_guidance: The following claims require outbound citations to authoritative sources: (1) The humectant/emollient/occlusive classification system — cite AAD (aad.org) or a peer-reviewed dermatology reference. (2) Fragrance as a leading cause of contact dermatitis — cite AAD or a published allergy/dermatology study. (3) Lauric acid as the primary fatty acid in coconut oil with emollient properties — cite a peer-reviewed source such as the Journal of Cosmetic Science or International Journal of Dermatology; name the mechanism ('lauric acid's emollient action via lipid replenishment of the stratum corneum') rather than a generic claim. (4) Parabens and endocrine-disruption concerns — cite NIEHS (niehs.nih.gov) or a published study; do NOT state this as settled consensus — frame as 'ongoing research suggests' or 'some studies have raised concerns'. (5) The 'fragrance-free vs. unscented' label distinction — cite FDA (fda.gov) or AAD. ABSOLUTE CLAIMS TO AVOID OR SOFTEN: Do not write 'proven to eliminate dry skin', 'guaranteed to work', or 'natural ingredients are always safer' — these cannot be supported and should be removed or reframed with qualified language. Do not claim coconut oil is universally non-comedogenic — evidence is mixed and this varies by skin type.
